tagline.text: The tallest bridge in the Philippines, 89 m above a deep ravine

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (about 20 minutes on the bridge itself)

children.text: Agas-Agas Bridge in Sogod, Southern Leyte, is a concrete bridge about 350 m long and 89 m high across a ravine, and it is known as the tallest bridge in the Philippines. There is no entrance fee, and it makes a good quick stop for views of the gorge from the highway.

Agas-Agas Bridge is a prestressed concrete beam bridge in Barangay Kahupian, Sogod, in the province of Southern Leyte on the southern part of Leyte Island. It carries the Pan-Philippine Highway (the national road running from Manila to Mindanao), and according to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) marker, the deck stands about
above the ravine floor and the total length is about
. The longest central span is
, held up by two piers that are
and
tall. Because of this height, it is often described as the tallest bridge in the Philippines.

The bridge was not planned primarily as a tourist attraction. This mountain stretch of road used to be cut off by frequent landslides during heavy rain and typhoons. The bridge was built to bypass that dangerous section and shorten driving time. Construction is known to have started on November 17, 2006 and finished on August 2, 2009, at a total cost of about
, partly funded by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA). It has two lanes, a design load limit of 20 tons, and a width of about

For travelers, this is more of a photo stop than a full destination. There are parking and viewing areas near the ends of the bridge, and there is no entrance fee. All you do is walk across and look down into the deep forested ravine on both sides, but walking this high above the ground on a road is not something you get to do often. Keep its place in your itinerary small. It fits best as a stop on the overland trip from Tacloban down to Maasin, or as part of a Sogod Bay itinerary.
One more thing to know about is the zipline that once ran beside the bridge. Zipline Leyte opened in April 2011, with twin cables about

long crossing diagonally above the bridge and the river. Its operating license lapsed in October 2014 and it has not carried passengers since. Only rusty cables and structures remain, so do not come here expecting to ride a zipline.

blocks.title: The tallest bridge in the Philippines

children.text: The deck is about

above the ravine floor, and the bridge is known as the tallest in the Philippines. The DPWH marker lists the height and length, which makes it a good place for a proof-of-visit photo. Some articles give the length as 400 m, but the official marker says about

The bridge is a two-lane road shared by vehicles and pedestrians. If you stay close to the railing, you can look down at the green ravine and the river below on both sides. Buses and trucks keep passing, so you must walk right next to the railing.

Several visitors report parking, restrooms, and small souvenir stalls at the south end of the bridge. From the provincial pavilion built by the local government, you can see the whole ravine at a glance. The stalls open only when there are enough visitors, so it is best to bring drinks with you.

blocks.title: Civil engineering built with Japanese support

children.text: This prestressed concrete beam bridge was completed in nearly three years with funding from Japan's JICA. The central span of
between the piers stands out in particular. If you are interested in civil engineering, you can see the pier height and deck structure up close.

blocks.title: A misty ravine in the morning

children.text: The ravine often fills with fog on rainy afternoons, but the morning view is usually clearer. If you arrive early, you can best see the clouds rising from the valley and the colors of the forest, and with less traffic it is easier to walk.

Parts of the zipline, which operated from 2011 to 2014, still remain. It is not operating and the cables are rusty, so do not go near it or climb on it, and treat it only as something to look at from a distance. You can ask the Kahupian barangay office whether it will ever reopen.

items.title: Day stop
items.subtitle: On the way from Tacloban to Maasin

children.text: Take a Duptours bus to Maasin from the New Transport Terminal in Tacloban. Tell the driver or conductor in advance that you want to get off at Agas-Agas Bridge.
After about
2 hours 30 minutes
from Tacloban, get off near the bridge. Walk slowly across the deck along the railing and look into the ravine on both sides.
Take photos and rest at the south parking and viewing area. Look at the zipline structures only from a distance.
Flag down a passing bus or van and continue toward Maasin. Buses will not wait for you, so it is best to plan your onward transport in advance.
If you rely only on public transport, your time at the bridge is short and the onward ride is uncertain. If possible, we recommend a rental car or a chartered vehicle.

items.title: By motorcycle from Sogod
items.subtitle: Using Sogod town as your base

children.text: At the Sogod bus terminal, take a habal-habal (motorcycle taxi) or a tricycle. It takes about
30 minutes
from Sogod town to the bridge. Be sure to agree on the fare before you ride.
Arrive at the bridge and walk across to enjoy the view.
If you asked the driver to wait, ride back to Sogod town with the same driver. Local articles mention a round-trip charter at around
Fares vary by season and by driver. Agree clearly on the round-trip price and the waiting time before you ride.
There are direct flights from Manila to Tacloban (TAC), taking about
1 hour 20 minutes
. Airlines and times change by season, so check when you book.
From Tacloban to the bridge it is about
2 hours 30 minutes
by road. Duptours buses to Maasin are known to run hourly from 06:00 to 17:00 from the New Transport Terminal in Tacloban. The fare from Tacloban to Maasin is about
Flight and bus schedules can change, so check with the operator before you leave.

items.title: By boat from Cebu to Maasin

children.text: You can fly from Manila to Cebu City first, then take an OceanJet fast craft from Cebu to Maasin. It departs daily at 07:00 and takes about
3 hours
, with fares reported at about
for tourist class and about
for business class.
From Maasin to the bridge it is about
1 hour 30 minutes
by bus or van heading toward Sogod or Tacloban, for a fare of about
Boat schedules and fares vary by season, so check with the operator before you leave.

items.title: The last stretch to the bridge

children.text: From Sogod town it is about
30 minutes
by habal-habal or tricycle. Visitors report a shared habal-habal fare of about
one way, but it varies by season and driver, so always settle the price first.
When riding a bus or van, tell the driver in advance to drop you just before the bridge. In front of the bridge there is no bus stop, only the highway shoulder.
A rental car or a chartered vehicle is the most convenient. Buses will not wait for passengers, so a vehicle is better if you want time to take photos and look around slowly.
The approach roads near the bridge can be blocked during heavy rain, so adjust your plans on bad-weather days.

You can visit the bridge all year round, but the view is what matters here. On rainy or foggy days you cannot see how deep the ravine is. Mornings are generally clear, while afternoons often bring fog and showers.
Leyte lies in the typhoon belt, so from June to November rain and wind are frequent and access roads are sometimes blocked. March to May is relatively dry and easier for getting around.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Cloudy days occur with the winter monsoon, so a morning visit is best.
Clear views make this the best time for photos and a walk on the bridge.
Landslides or closed access roads are possible, so check the weather and road conditions.

items.label: Entrance fee
items.note: It is a highway bridge with no separate entrance fee, and the viewing area and parking are also free

items.label: Lodging (Sogod)
items.note: A simple hotel in town for one night; rates vary by season

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.

There is no lodging around the bridge, and the nearest base is Sogod town. In Sogod there is a simple but tidy option such as GV Hotel on Osmeña Street, within walking distance of the bus terminal. In Southern Leyte, many people also stay overnight in Maasin City or Tacloban and travel from there. Room rates change by season, so check locally.

Eating is most reliable in the restaurants of Sogod or Maasin town. The stalls next to the bridge open only when there are many visitors, so expect only simple drinks and souvenirs. It is a rural road in the Philippines, so having lunch in town before or after is the easier plan.
About
20 minutes
on the bridge is enough. It is a place to stop on the way, not one to plan half a day around.
If you go early in the morning, the view is clear and there is little traffic. On rainy afternoons the ravine is often foggy and there is less to see.
This is a real highway. Buses and trucks keep passing, so walk right up against the railing and do not stand in the lane to take photos.
If you go by public transport, buses will not wait for you. Decide your return ride and time in advance.
For a habal-habal or tricycle, agree on the price before you ride, and if it is a round trip, state clearly how long it will wait.
Bring water, a hat, and a light snack. The stalls open only when there are many people.
We found no official drone ban, but the height difference between the valley floor and the launch point is very large, so fly carefully and check local conditions first.
Do not go for the zipline. It has not operated since 2014. You can ask the Kahupian barangay office (0905 925 2523) about the latest status.
The bridge is a highway with constant traffic, so do not stop in the lane or lean out over the railing. Heavy rain can block the approach roads.
It is high and the railing may feel low, so children must hold an adult's hand when walking.
Do not climb on or touch the rusty zipline cables and steel structures. The facility is no longer operating.
If you arrive by bus and do not say in advance where to get off, you may be carried past it. The front of the bridge is not an official stop.
After heavy rain or a typhoon, approach roads can be blocked, so check the latest weather and road information.
It is a public road with no set admission or opening hours, so whether the stalls or restrooms are available can vary from day to day.
This is the sea of Southern Leyte lying to the south of the bridge, known for wall diving off Padre Burgos. It pairs well with the bridge for a one- or two-day itinerary.
This is the longest bridge over water in the Philippines, linking Tacloban in northern Leyte with Samar Island. You can compare the two bridges when planning your Leyte trip.
In Pintuyan to the south, whale sharks can usually be seen from November to May. The 2025–2026 season closed on June 1, 2026, and reopening is expected around October. Check the timing locally.
A small island you can reach by public boat from Padre Burgos. Check boat times locally.
